source: What Child Is This - We Voice (Part 1 of 2), Entry 9

blocks.text: 09: WHY IS THE CHRISTMAS STORY FULL OF WOMEN WHO SHOULD NOT HAVE BEEN PART OF IT?

sentences: Matthew opens his gospel with a genealogy.
We established in Entry 5 that the genealogy isn't a dry data set but a theological argument, structured with intentional precision.
We noted that Matthew condenses his list into three groups of fourteen, encodes the name of David in the structure, and uses the list to make the claim that Jesus is the promised Messianic heir.
What we didn't fully examine is who Matthew includes in that list when he didn't have to.
Ancient genealogies, particularly Jewish genealogies constructed to establish royal or priestly lineage, were lists of men.
The line ran father to son to grandson.
Women didn't appear in these lists because women didn't inherit title or throne in the normal course of Jewish social and legal practice.
A genealogy was a record of patrilineal descent, and the inclusion of mothers wasn't the convention.
Matthew knew this.
He was writing to a Jewish audience that knew this.
Matthew includes five women anyway.
The first is Tamar.
Her story is in Genesis chapter thirty-eight.
Tamar was the daughter-in-law of Judah, one of the twelve sons of Jacob.

After her husband died and Judah failed to follow the law of levirate marriage by giving her his third son as a husband, Tamar disguised herself as a prostitute, slept with Judah her father-in-law, and became pregnant with twins.
One of those twins, Perez, carries the line forward to David and eventually to Jesus.
Tamar's entry into the lineage comes through a morally catastrophic encounter involving deception, incest, and the failure of an entire family to do what the law required.
The second is Rahab.
Her story is in Joshua chapter two.
Rahab was a Canaanite prostitute living in Jericho who hid the Israelite spies when Joshua sent them to scout the city before the conquest.
She made a bargain for her family's survival and kept her word.

She's one of the most unlikely figures in the entire Old Testament to appear in the Messianic lineage, both because she was a Gentile and because her occupation is stated plainly in the text with no softening.
The third is Ruth.
Her story occupies its own book.
Ruth was a Moabite woman, again a Gentile, who married into a Jewish family, lost her husband, and chose to follow her mother-in-law Naomi back to Bethlehem rather than return to her own people.
Her loyalty to Naomi is one of the most moving portraits in Scripture.
She's also a foreigner in the lineage of a Messiah whose covenant was established with the Jewish nation.
The fourth is Bathsheba, though Matthew doesn't use her name.
He says Solomon's mother had been Uriah's wife.
That circumlocution is doing significant work.
It identifies Bathsheba not by her own name but by her first husband, the man King David had killed.

The story is one of the darkest in the Old Testament: David saw Bathsheba, sent for her, slept with her, and when she became pregnant, arranged for Uriah to be placed in the front lines of battle where he would be killed.
The child of that union died.
Solomon, who succeeded David and carries the line to Jesus, was Bathsheba's second son.
Matthew could have said Solomon's mother.
He said Uriah's wife.
The fifth is Mary.
These five women form a pattern, and Matthew is building it deliberately.
All five are involved in pregnancies or conceptions that are irregular, scandalous, legally complicated, socially precarious, or some combination of all four.
None of them fit the profile of a woman a first-century Jewish genealogist would include in a royal lineage if his goal were to construct a clean and credible record.
A woman involved in incest with her father-in-law.
A Canaanite prostitute.
A foreign widow from a people the law regarded with suspicion.
A woman whose first husband was murdered by the king who then became her husband.
A teenage girl pregnant during betrothal whose story required divine intervention to explain.
Matthew includes all five.
He isn't trying to hide them.
He's pointing at them.
The pattern they share is precisely the pattern Mary's conception completes.
Every one of these women was in a situation that looked, by the standards of her community and her time, like a problem.
Every one of those situations produced something that carried the line of promise forward.
Tamar's deception produced the twin who became the ancestor of David.
Rahab's choice to protect the spies produced the family line that reached Boaz.
Ruth's loyalty produced Obed, father of Jesse, father of David.
Bathsheba's terrible story produced Solomon.
Mary's impossible pregnancy produced Jesus.
Matthew is making a theological argument that has been running through the entire Old Testament and is now arriving at its conclusion.
God doesn't work exclusively through respectable channels, clean circumstances, and conventionally acceptable arrangements.
He has been working through complicated, broken, irregular, and humanly unlikely situations since the beginning.
The lineage of the Messiah is the record of that pattern, and Mary's place at the end of it isn't an anomaly.
She's the culmination of it.
The evidentiary question this entry presses is the same one we've been pressing across Movement Two.
No one inventing a Messianic lineage to establish the credentials of a religious movement includes this list of women.

A fabricator constructing a royal genealogy for a messianic figure in the first century Jewish world would include the most respectable, most legally clean, most socially unimpeachable female figures available to him.
He might include a famous matriarch.
He wouldn't include the woman who slept with her father-in-law.
He wouldn't include a Canaanite prostitute.
He wouldn't include a Moabite foreigner.
He wouldn't identify a queen mother by the name of the husband the previous king had murdered.
He wouldn't do any of this because none of it serves the goal of making the lineage look good.
Matthew does all of it, and he does it in the opening paragraph of his gospel, the first thing his Jewish audience reads.
He isn't embarrassed by any of these women.
He's holding them up, because the point he's making isn't that the lineage is clean.
The point is that the lineage is real, and that God's pattern of working through impossible circumstances has been consistent from the beginning.
Mary's impossible conception isn't a departure from how God operates.
It's entirely in keeping with how He has always operated, from Tamar through Rahab through Ruth through Bathsheba to Mary.
The five women in Matthew's genealogy aren't a problem for the Christmas story.
They're the strongest argument in it.
Matthew could have omitted all five women from his genealogy without any loss of the genealogical argument he was making.
Ancient Jewish genealogies didn't typically include women at all.
Why would a writer constructing a document designed to establish Jesus's Messianic credentials choose to include five women whose stories would raise questions rather than answer them?
The pattern across all five women is irregular circumstances that God works through to carry the line of promise forward.
If Matthew is pointing at that pattern deliberately, what is he asking his Jewish audience to conclude about Mary's irregular circumstance specifically?
Matthew identifies Bathsheba not by her name but as Uriah's wife, keeping the murder of Uriah in the genealogy of Jesus even when he didn't have to.
What does the decision to preserve that detail rather than smooth it over tell us about what kind of document Matthew intended his genealogy to be?
